title: Made ’Em Myself
dateline: The city. The day after the team test.
mood: A day of shopping that goes wrong, a night of burned fingers, and two small stars on a sunny roof.

hero.alt: On a sunny city roof a pink-haired girl in black gloves fixes a small gold star at the collar of a black-haired girl, who looks out at the viewer.

segs.t: Guinevere came out of the third shop with a coat over her arm and a phone case between her teeth.
She put both into Vexana’s hands. “Hold these. We won, so we’re shopping.”
“That isn’t how it works.”
“It is today.”
Vexana had stopped in the arcade’s first doorway as if she needed leave to go in. Her cloth bag hung on her shoulder, toolbox and all.
She brought the toolbox,
thought Guinevere.
Shopping.
Two House guards kept a shop’s distance behind them. Guinevere had stopped seeing them years ago. Today she had someone to buy things for.
Vexana’s own coat was worn shiny at the cuffs.
Not after today.
At a counter of hair things Guinevere found a clip shaped like a star. She tried it in her own hair at the mirror. Then she held it against Vexana’s.
Vexana’s hair was so black that the little star looked lit.
Guinevere held it there and turned to the girl at the counter. “I wonder if this would suit Vexana, too.”
Vexana had gone very still.
Guinevere paid with a black card before Vexana could open her mouth. A small gold crest sat in its corner: House Baroque. Vexana’s eyes stayed on it.
“Wait here,” said Guinevere. “I need shoes.”
In the middle of the arcade, a fabric stall sold felt in squares, every color. One was the pink of Guinevere’s hair.
Vexana stopped.
The Academy paid every cadet a small stipend. Hers lay in the toolbox’s bottom tray, still in its paper bands. She had never spent any of it.
She picked up the pink square. It was soft under her glove.
“I wonder if Guinevere would like this too.”
“Everybody likes that one,” said the stallholder.
The pink looked wrong on its own. Vexana took a square of black as well.
She set the cloth bag down, opened the toolbox and broke the first paper band. The stallholder wrapped the felt in brown paper.
Guinevere came back with a shoe box of her own. By then Vexana had buttoned her coat over the brown paper.
That night the bags covered the floor of Vexana’s room. It had never held so many things.
She folded each one back the way the shop had folded it. The star clip went last, back onto its little card. She held it a moment longer than the rest.
Then she wrote a note in small square letters.
I cannot repay this.
A coat was a debt. Everything anyone gave you was.
I owe him a life,
she thought.
I’m still paying it back in Enders. I can’t owe her too.
The black card had carried the Baroque crest, the first name on the fountain’s plaque.
Her House pays for everything here. Not for me.
The felt lay on her desk in its brown paper. That was for someone else, so it was no debt. She put it in her drawer.
Before dawn she carried the bags down the corridor to Guinevere’s door. It stood open a hand’s width. Inside, a drone’s ring glowed on its charger.
She set the bags against the wall with the note on top. She did not look in.
Guinevere stepped out for the morning run and nearly fell over them.
Every bag was folded shop-neat. On top lay a note.
I cannot repay this.
Once, on her father’s birthday, she had left a cake on the bench outside his office. In the morning the plate was back on the bench. Washed.
Her hands had gone cold.
Vexana came round the corner in her running things and stopped.
“What is this?” said Guinevere.
“I can’t repay it.”
“It’s a present! Nobody repays a present!”
“Someone always does.”
“It’s only money!”
“I am not something you buy,” said Vexana.
The note crumpled in Guinevere’s fist.
Bought.
Under the brass plaque, two cadets had used that word.
Her score was bought.
And her father answered everything with money. He had lost her mother and bought walls. He had never once come out of his office.
She’s the one who said I was strong,
she thought.
And all she sees is his money.
“Fine,” she said. She picked up every bag. “Fine!”
She went back into her room and shut the door all the way, which she never did.
All that day she did not speak to Vexana. She did it loudly.
“I’m not speaking to you,” she told her at the run, from the far side of the fountain. She told her again at drills, and twice at lunch.
Her drones trailed after her with their ears flat.
Across the training hall Vexana did her fifty forms and never once looked over. That was worse.
That night Guinevere sat on her bed and turned the black card over in her fingers. The little crest caught the lamp.
Even the guards’ cakes had come out of the House kitchen.
Everything I ever gave anybody,
she thought,
he paid for.
Then I’ll make her something. Money can’t solder.
She got up and took her drones’ spares box down from the shelf.
The repair room behind the training hall had a hooded lamp and a soldering iron that nobody liked.
Guinevere had never soldered anything in her life.
From the spares box she took a strip of thin gold plate.
Stars,
she thought. Vexana had gone so still over that clip.
Two came out of the plate, five points each, their edges filed smooth.
The first seam would not take. The second took, and so did her fingertip. She hissed, sucked it and went on.
By the fourth seam she had band-aids on three fingers. By the eighth, on five.
At two in the morning her phone buzzed beside the iron. She knew who it was. She let it buzz until it stopped.
The last seam came out a hair crooked. She lifted the iron to do it again.
Outside, the dawn bell rang.
Then that one’s mine,
she thought.
She held the two stars up under the lamp, in fingers wrapped to the knuckle. “A miracle, with my own hands.”
Beside her, the drones’ ears came up.
That morning a plan came under Vexana’s door, one line in gold.
The roof. Noon. (Please.)
She had not slept. All the day before, through fifty forms, she had heard herself in the corridor.
Something you buy.
At the fountain the word had been
bought
, and she had known it for a lie.
Late last night the back window of the training hall had stayed lit. She had phoned once. Nobody answered.
The dormitory roof was flat and hot, with washing lines and green guardrails. Under the dome the sky was clear blue. The city ran away below them, roof after roof, down to the bay.
Guinevere stood at the rail with her hands behind her back. Her drones hung at her shoulders, ears high.
“The coat,” Vexana began.
“Forget the coat.” Guinevere brought her hands round. Two small gold stars lay on her palm. “Look at this! I made a suuuper amazing invention! With this, we’ll battle side-by-side forever!”
Vexana looked at the fingertips first. Band-aids were wrapped round five of them.
The wrapped fingers curled under. Then Guinevere pushed her palm out further.
“Here! I made ’em myself, ya know!” said Guinevere.
The wind moved the washing on the lines.
“They’re called Emblems of Hope,” said Guinevere. “I named them too.”
She pinned one to Vexana’s collar. Her wrapped fingers fumbled the pin twice. She pinned the other to her own.
“There. Now we match.”
A girl with two braids had said that once, at the Shield’s home, holding out a blue ribbon. Vexana had said no.
“They’re meant to light up,” said Guinevere, quickly. “It needs two of us. I couldn’t test it.”
Both stars stayed dark.
Vexana pulled off her right glove. She turned the star at her collar with a bare fingertip.
On the back the solder had run, been filed down and run again. She knew that kind of work, and what solder did to fingertips. One seam ran a hair crooked.
Nobody had ever made her anything.
She sat up all night,
thought Vexana.
Because of what I said.
“Oh no, that’s the bad one.” Guinevere reached for it. “That one’s supposed to be mine. Give it here.”
“No,” said Vexana.
Her bare hand stayed over the star. Guinevere’s hand stopped in the air.
It needs two of us,
Vexana thought.
This one, I can pay for. I only have to be the other one.
“In the corridor I used their word,” said Vexana. “The fountain’s word. It was a lie in my mouth too.”
Guinevere looked at her. Then she looked out over the rail, and her ears went pink.
“Well,” she said. “The coat I picked was very ugly.”
At Guinevere’s collar, the star began to glow.
Vexana looked down. Hers was glowing too, soft and gold, and warm against her collarbone.
Neither of them moved. Then Guinevere squeaked. She snatched out her phone. “Don’t move. Don’t you dare move.”
She held it out at arm’s length and leaned in close. In the little screen were two faces, and a gold star lit at each collar.
“Look, they light up when our powers are in sync,” said Guinevere.
Vexana looked at the girl in the screen with the lit star at her throat. She did not look away.

blocks.caption: Two faces in the little screen.

media.alt: At the green rail of a rooftop high over the city, Guinevere holds her phone up at arm's length for a selfie with Vexana, a small gold star at each collar.

segs.t: Guinevere leaned on the green rail.
“We protect this world,” she said. “The two of us.”
Vexana looked out at the city a long while.
“A promise,” she said.
Guinevere’s grin came back all at once. “I built in one more trick. Go and stand at the far rail.”
Vexana went. At the far rail both stars were silent.
She walked back. Halfway across the roof, both stars gave a small beep.
She looked at Guinevere, and walked back to the far rail. Silence. She came back. Beep.
She did it three more times, with a straight face. She counted.
“Stop that,” said Guinevere. She was laughing.
Vexana stopped beside her. Her bare fingertip went back to the crooked seam.
“It works,” she said.
